clinicalPearls: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, typically presenting between 3 and 6 weeks of age and more common in firstborn males.
The hallmark is progressive, forceful non-bilious (projectile) vomiting shortly after feeds, with the infant remaining hungry and eager to feed again.
The classic metabolic picture is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid and chloride.
A palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium/right upper quadrant and visible gastric peristalsis are classic but not always present.
Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, demonstrating a thickened and elongated pyloric muscle.
The vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater; bilious vomiting should prompt consideration of other diagnoses.
Initial management is medical resuscitation: correcting dehydration and the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance before any operation.
Definitive treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy, which is not an emergency and should follow adequate fluid and electrolyte correction.
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus narrows and elongates the pyloric channel, obstructing gastric emptying. The exact cause is unknown but involves genetic and environmental factors. Persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; ongoing losses and renal compensation drive potassium loss and, later, paradoxical aciduria. Fluid losses cause dehydration. The obstruction is proximal to the biliary drainage, so vomitus is non-bilious.
additionalDifferentials: Metabolic disorders or raised intracranial pressure causing vomiting
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound to measure pyloric muscle thickness and channel length
Blood gas to characterise the alkalosis
Assessment of hydration status and weight
redFlags: Signs of significant dehydration or shock
Bilious vomiting, which points away from pyloric stenosis toward a surgical emergency such as volvulus
Lethargy or reduced responsiveness from dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after appropriate resuscitation and pyloromyotomy, with prompt recovery and no long-term gastrointestinal sequelae.
pitfalls: Rushing to surgery before correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities
Mistaking the illness for simple reflux or overfeeding and delaying diagnosis
Overlooking that vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, and failing to reconsider the diagnosis if it is bilious
Underestimating the degree of dehydration and metabolic alkalosis
management: Correct dehydration and the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with intravenous fluid and potassium replacement before any operation, as surgery is never an emergency until the infant is rehydrated and biochemically corrected
Decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube and keep the infant nil by mouth pending surgery
Perform definitive Ramstedt pyloromyotomy once resuscitation is complete
Reintroduce graded enteral feeds postoperatively as tolerated
Monitor serial electrolytes, chloride, bicarbonate and hydration until normalised
